look_here_first: KNOTGRASS / WETLAND PASPALUM: often TWO narrow one-sided V-shaped flowering racemes, but that alone is not a species ID. It spreads in wet ground by surface STOLONS that root at nodes. The original photo proves the two-raceme V; the NEW licensed meadow photo shows low mat-like habit but does NOT prove individual rooted nodes. Separate from P. notatum (bahia grass) with a true runner and mature spikelet anatomy.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Search actual growing horizontal stems and root-bearing nodes, rather than interpreting two racemes alone. Bahia grass P. notatum also often makes two racemes; grass-root habit and mature upper-glume/spikelet measurements must corroborate. The Australian wetland image is not proof of Texas nativity.
do_not_use_alone: Number of racemes without the entire flowering axis
Habitat, height, or vegetative tuft in isolation
Microscopic glume hairs or spikelet length inferred from a photo without scale

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Paspalum: what to inspect
steps: Pair the two-raceme photo with a legal close field photo exposing a rooted aboveground stolon node and centimeter ruler. Photograph complete leaf collar and a ripened spikelet; preserve geography and nativity uncertainty.
First show the WHOLE head, then ONE one-sided raceme and attached spikelets. Never treat a photograph of one branch as total raceme count.
Obtain a real intact mature spikelet and measure it with 1-mm reference; use margin hair pattern and glumes to separate close Paspalum taxa.
Photograph blade/sheath joint and same-plant rootstock; knotgrass needs actually rooted horizontal stolons, not merely a low mat.
If plant photo is source-labelled only, keep identity tentative and leave existing county-native fields unchanged.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Knotgrass combines wet-ground creeping stolons with usually paired (rarely three) unilateral flowering racemes. Bahia grass can produce two racemes but differs in low turf/rhizome architecture and spikelet structure. Thin paspalum may form just one or a few flowering branches but has different leafy habit and varietal hair traits; Florida paspalum forms robust upright bunches and bigger oval spikelets.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Gross photo structures are references, NOT expert confirmation. Even new licensed images are PROVISIONAL — USER PHOTO REVIEW PENDING and not proof of Hays County presence.

diagnostic_species_finalization_20261023.look_here_first: KNOTGRASS: find a low wet-ground perennial with real creeping aboveground stolons rooting at nodes, then usually TWO (occasionally 1 or 3) narrow, one-sided racemes making a V. Verify 2.4–4 mm mature plano-convex spikelets in two rows; the lower glume is absent or a tiny scale. Two racemes alone do NOT establish this species because bahiagrass also commonly has a V-shaped head.

measured_diagnostic_key.character: Stoloniferous, mat-forming perennial in damp soil; actual rooted nodes required, not inferred from a flat photo.
Usually 2, occasionally 1 or 3; about 2–8 cm long, one-sided spikelet rows; narrowly winged rachis.
measured_diagnostic_key.source: Flora of New Zealand; Kew GrassBase via AusGrass

measured_diagnostic_key.character: Usually about 2.4–4 mm long, solitary (rarely paired), plano-convex; one lower sterile and one upper fertile floret; no true long awns.
Usually absent or vestigial; if present a short hyaline scale, variable, not a long normal glume.
measured_diagnostic_key.source: USDA IDTools; Flora of New Zealand

measured_diagnostic_key.character: Approximately 2.6–3.6 mm, generally spikelet-length, usually 3–5 veins, finely appressed-hairy.
Approximately 2.6–3.6 mm, 3–5 veins, generally glabrous, not the hardened fertile grain cover.
Approximately 2.4–3.6 mm in AusGrass (2–3 mm in USDA IDTools); hardened, pale, awnless, often minutely hairy near tip.

Membranous, white; up to 1.6 mm in Florida treatment, 2–3 mm in Flora of China description. Different floras report different lengths; photograph actual inner blade–sheath junction with 1-mm scale. Hair tufts on sheath edge are NOT the ligule.

crew_sequence: Trace the stem to a visible root-bearing horizontal stolon node; distinguish stolon from an arching flowering culm.
Count complete attached one-sided racemes on one head; photograph the shared branch point.
At 10–20× measure five ripe spikelets and dissect a representative unit into upper glume, lower sterile lemma and hardened upper fertile lemma.
Expose inner ligule and adjacent collar with 1-mm scale; check sheath-margin hairs separately.
If rooting nodes or spikelets cannot be verified, record Paspalum sp. rather than species-certified P. distichum.

local_lookalikes.separation: Also frequently two racemes: do not identify from V shape; inspect rooted growth, rachis, spikelet shape and mature glumes.
Tufted or shortly rhizomatous, often paired smaller 1.4–2.6 mm spikelets and very short 0.2–0.5 mm membranous ligule; not a wet-ground long-stolon mat.
Usually a robust tuft with several racemes and conspicuously silky-margined larger spikelets; avoid raceme count as a sole character.
